newsitem.title: USA: PRESS DIGEST - Wall Street Journal - April 11.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - Wall Street Journal - April 11.

text.p: The following stories were reported in Friday's electronic version of The Wall Street Journal:
* Boeing has plans to provide heavy-maintenance services to large airlines in a bid to diversify, according to people familiar with the matter.
* Mutual fund investors have in the past few days boosted their purchases of stock funds after holding back in March.
* A pact between Nippon Credit and Bankers Trust for Nippon to assign Bankers management of some overseas clients could herald opportunities for U.S. banks in Japan.
* A United Auto Workers strike at an engine plant forced Chrysler to shut four of its light-truck factories.
* Sears said it would refund money collected from some of its credit card holders who filed for bankruptcy and said resolving the matter would have a "material effect" on 1997 earnings.
* U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin expressed "concern" about the dollar's rise against the yen.
* Retailers' March same-store sales rose about four percent with many apparel companies showing weak gains.
* McDonald's plans to give away popular beanbag toy animal Teenie Beenie Babies with its Happy Meals.
* SBC Communications is seen seeking permission to enter the long-distance market.
* The Dow Jones industrials declined 23.79 to 6,540.05 in light trade.
* An advertising industry panel failed to resolve a U.S. Postal Service complaint about a Federal Express radio campaign and the matter went to the Federal Trade Commission.
* General Electric's net income rose 11 percent in the first quarter to $1.68 billion.
* Intel is set to announce computer chip price cuts which are steeper than usual at the end of April.
* J.P. Morgan and First Union both posted slightly better-than-expected quarterly earnings.
* Donald Trump received a pay package worth $7 million in 1996, including a $5 million bonus.
* US Airways told workers the airline's growth strategy was being paralyzed by a failure to agree on contract concessions.
* Washington Mutual, in a takeover bid with H.F. Ahmanson for Great Western Financial, pledged $75 billion in inner city loans over 10 years.
* Heard on the Street: You can't watch high-definition television yet, but don't be surprised if your broker starts calling and trying to sell you the stocks now.
* Credit markets: Bond prices scarcely budged for a second consecutive day, as the market awaited a key government report today: the Commerce Department's estimate of monthly growth in retail sales.
((New York newsdesk 212-859-1610))
